topic.title: We log in to the sale and log out without buying
topic.claim: This Diwali the sale is a place to browse, because the prices went up and the discounts got smaller, so the cart became a wishlist.
topic.behaviour: You open the app, fill the cart with the TV or phone, check it twice over three days, and close it. The order count stays huge because small things still get bought.
topic.mechanism: Prices on appliances rose before the festive sales, so a discount is cut from a higher starting number. Salaries did not move, so the big purchase waits.
topic.group: Salaried Indians planning a big festive purchase
topic.moment: Your cart has the ₹50,000 TV in it, and it has had it for a week.

turn.believed: Festive sales are when Indians splurge.
turn.actually: They still show up and order small things, but the big ticket waits, because the goalposts moved while the pay stayed put.

topic.because: Platforms need traffic and orders to look healthy, so they keep the show running. Households quietly pay the extra and decide what can wait.

proof.fact: Datum put online sales at ₹29,800-₹30,900 Cr, down 7-10% from ₹33,200 Cr a year earlier, while Redseer saw nearly 100 Mn shoppers placing more than 350 Mn orders.
Prices of TVs, air conditioners, refrigerators and washing machines were set to rise 5% to 8% from October 1, so a ₹50,000 TV would cost ₹2,500 to ₹4,000 more.

topic.payoff: A sale only counts if the final price is below last year's final price. Check that before you check the percentage.
topic.send_to: The friend who is 'waiting for the Diwali sale' on a fridge
real_details: Sachin Taparia said 'Household earnings are not rising, and inflation continues to rise.'
The page cites an Economic Times report that festive discounts were 35-40% lower than last year.
topic.news_peg: Festive sales first-leg data, Oct 8-18, reported 2026-10-23
topic.why_now: Dhanteras and Diwali are days away and the big-ticket decision is being made right now.

score.why: The cart became a wishlist because pay stayed put; the ₹50,000 TV waiting a week is a familiar moment.

topic.villain: a sale calendar that moves the goalposts while the paycheck stays put

violations: Slide 5: "That's millions of carts like yours, waiting." No source or proof says millions of carts are being held back. The sources give lower sales and order counts, not abandoned or waiting carts. That makes it an invented figure and an unsupported claim about the world.

Slide 5: "The platforms are fine either way." This is a mechanism stated as fact, and it clashes with the post's own data that online festive sales came in below last year. "The sum the countdown hopes you'll skip" also implies a deliberate plan that can't be shown. The topic's actual because is that platforms need traffic and orders to look healthy, so they keep the show running.
notes: slide 5: Rewrite the because. Say plainly that the platforms need the order count and the traffic to look healthy, so the countdown banners and small-ticket deals keep running. Households quietly pay the higher price or put the big item off. Delete "fine either way", "the sum the countdown hopes you'll skip" and "millions of carts like yours". The sales-below-last-year fact can stay once, plainly stated.

slides 3 and 4: These two slides partly do the same job, since both are about "looks busy, big stuff is stuck". Tighten the pair so slide 3 carries the small-things-go-through behaviour with the order count, and slide 4 carries only the price rise and the TV now costing more. Keep the numbers to two. The one-line explanation of why orders look huge while the TV waits is the best new idea, so give it room.

slide 4: The turn only half lands, because the post never names the belief it's flipping. Add one short beat that Diwali sales are supposed to be when we splurge, and that this year the big purchase is what waits. sources.fact: Redseer estimated festive e-commerce GMV of about Rs 24,000 crore and 8-9 crore orders in the first two days of the 2026 sale, with purchases pulled forward on expected price rises. This is strong demand rather than a browse-only sale, and the page says nothing about discounts or abandoned carts.

cover.headline: This Diwali sale, your cart turned into a [wishlist]
cover.sub: The sale is still running. The big purchase is waiting.

paragraphs: This Diwali sale, your cart turned into a wishlist.
slides.why_swipe: Whose cart, and what's sitting in it?

paragraphs: The TV has been in your cart for a week now. You open the app on the ride home, phone warm in your palm, and check the price again.
In the lift, as the doors creak shut, a banner flashes: "Deal ends at midnight." You close the app. Again.
slides.why_swipe: So what did you actually buy this sale?

paragraphs: The small stuff goes through in one tap. A phone cover, a strip of fairy lights, the shoes that were marked way down.
The doorbell rings all week, your share of the millions of orders. Each box feels like you shopped. The TV doesn't move.
slides.why_swipe: If everyone is ordering, why is the TV still sitting there?

paragraphs: Late one night you open the cart again. In September this TV was ₹50,000. Tonight the number under the deal tag is ₹2,500 to ₹4,000 higher.
**You read the tag, not the number under it.**
slides.why_swipe: Why is the number higher in the middle of a sale?

paragraphs: TVs, ACs and fridges were set to cost a bit more from October. The discount gets cut from that raised price. Your pay didn't rise with it.
**The deal tag sits on a price that didn't exist a month ago.**
slides.why_swipe: So is the sale a con, or are you just being careful?

paragraphs: The countdown banners keep running all week. The orders keep coming. Total online festive sales still slipped below last year.
You enjoy the scrolling, though. Late-night deals feel like a small treat. But every time the TV comes up, you feel stretched, and you push it to "after bonus".
slides.why_swipe: So where does this end up?

paragraphs: Dhanteras comes. Your phone buzzes on the desk: "Still thinking about it?"
You open the app. "Huge discount." You try to remember what this TV cost last Diwali. You can't.
**The discount is the only number on the screen you're sure of.**

end.save: Open this again on Dhanteras, right before you tap 'Place order' on anything big.
end.send: Send to the friend who has been 'waiting for the Diwali sale' on a fridge since August.
end.promise: How money really moves in India.

draft.caption: What's been sitting in your cart since the sale started, and what is it waiting for?
draft.alt_text: Instagram carousel. Cover: 'This Diwali sale, your cart turned into a wishlist.' The slides follow a reader who keeps a TV in their online cart for a week, checking the price on the ride home, then closing the app in the lift when a 'Deal ends at midnight' banner flashes. Small things like a phone cover, fairy lights and shoes go through in one tap, part of the millions of orders, while the TV doesn't move. Late one night the reader sees that the TV, ₹50,000 in September, now costs ₹2,500 to ₹4,000 more under the deal tag, thumb hovering over 'Place order'. Prices of TVs, ACs and fridges were set to rise a bit from October, so the discount is cut from a raised price while pay stayed the same. Countdown banners keep running even as total online festive sales slip below last year. The reader enjoys scrolling deals but feels stretched and pushes the TV to 'after bonus'. On Dhanteras the phone buzzes: 'Still thinking about it?' The app shows 'Huge discount', and the reader can't remember what the TV cost last Diwali. The discount is the only number they're sure of.

claims.text: The festive sale crossed 350 million orders (Redseer: more than 350 million orders from nearly 100 million shoppers).
A ₹50,000 TV would cost ₹2,500 to ₹4,000 more after the October price rise.
Prices of TVs, ACs and fridges were set to rise 5% to 8% from October 1.
Total online festive sales came in below last year (Datum: down 7% to 10%).
